micro.title: Prefix sums and Kadane — subarrays without re-adding

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Day 1's running sum comes back with two superpowers.

✍️ **Prefix sums.** Store every running total in `pre` (with a leading 0). Any range sum is `pre[r+1] − pre[l]` in O(1). Draw the boundary picture once ([[ps-prefix-sum-basics#index-convention]]).
✍️ **Prefix sum + hash map.** "Subarray sum = k" means "two prefixes differ by k" — that is Two Sum on prefix sums. Seed the map with `{0: 1}` ([[ps-prefix-sum-hashmap#seed]]).
✍️ **Why not a sliding window?** Negative numbers make window sums non-monotone ([[sw-monotonicity-requirement#counterexample]]).
✍️ **Kadane.** Best subarray *ending here* = max(x, best ending at the previous index + x) ([[kad-kadane#idea]]). And its cousin: for "buy then sell", the best buy day is the minimum so far ([[kad-min-so-far#idea]]).
- Sums get big → `long` ([[cpp-integer-overflow#where]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ PREFIX SUM — `pre[0]=0; pre[i+1]=pre[i]+a[i]`; sum(l..r) = pre[r+1] − pre[l].
✍️ PREFIX + MAP — trigger "count subarrays with sum k" (negatives ok). cnt{0:1}; ans += cnt[run−k]; cnt[run]++.
✍️ KADANE — cur = max(x, cur+x); best = max(best, cur); init with a[0].
✍️ MIN SO FAR — profit = x − minSoFar; then minSoFar = min(minSoFar, x).

drill.title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
drill.statement: Add up the sums of every contiguous subarray whose length is odd.
drill.approach: With prefix sums, each odd-length subarray sum is O(1) → O(n²) total. O(n) trick: element i appears in ((i+1)(n−i)+1)/2 odd-length subarrays; sum a[i] × that count.
drill.trigger: "sum over many subarrays" → prefix sums, or count how many subarrays each element belongs to.
drill.details:
**Task.** Consider every contiguous subarray whose length is odd (1, 3, 5, …). Return the sum of all their sums.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 100; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000. Follow-up: O(n).

**Example:** `[1, 4, 2, 5, 3]` → `58`. The length-1 subarrays add up to 15. The length-3 ones are 7, 11 and 10, so 28. The length-5 one is 15. 15 + 28 + 15 = 58.

drill.title: Find the Pivot Integer
drill.statement: Find x in 1..n such that 1 + … + x equals x + … + n, or −1.
drill.approach: Left = x(x+1)/2, right = total − left + x; scan x, or solve x² = n(n+1)/2 directly.
drill.trigger: "sum on the left equals sum on the right" → prefix sum + total (Pivot Index).
drill.details:
**Task.** Given a positive integer n, find the integer x with 1 ≤ x ≤ n such that the sum 1 + 2 + … + x equals the sum x + (x+1) + … + n. Return x, or −1 if there is none. There is at most one such x.

**Input:** an integer `n`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `n = 8` → `6` (1+…+6 = 21 = 6+7+8). `n = 1` → `1`. `n = 4` → `-1`.

drill.title: Maximum Score After Splitting a String
drill.statement: Split a binary string into two non-empty parts; score = zeros in the left part + ones in the right part. Return the best score.
drill.approach: Count all ones first; walk split points keeping zeros-so-far and ones-so-far; score = zerosLeft + (totalOnes − onesLeft). Keep both parts non-empty.
drill.trigger: "split into left and right, score each side" → one running prefix and one total.
drill.details:
**Task.** A string of 0s and 1s is cut into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part. The score is the number of 0s in the left part plus the number of 1s in the right part. Return the best score over all possible cuts.

**Input:** a binary string `s`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 500.

**Example:** `"011101"` → `5`. Cutting after the first character gives `"0"` + `"11101"`: one zero plus four ones. `"00111"` → `5`.

drill.title: Number of Ways to Split Array
drill.statement: Count split points where the sum of the left part is at least the sum of the right part (both parts non-empty).
drill.approach: Total first; running left sum; at each split i (0..n−2) check left ≥ total − left. Sums up to 10¹⁰ → long.
drill.trigger: "left sum vs right sum at every split" → running prefix + total.
drill.details:
**Task.** A split at index i (0 ≤ i < n − 1) divides the array into `nums[0..i]` and `nums[i+1..n−1]`, so both parts are non-empty. It is valid when the left part's sum is at least the right part's sum. Count the valid splits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 10⁵; −10⁵ ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[10, 4, -8, 7]` → `2`. The splits give 10 vs 3 (valid), 14 vs −1 (valid) and 6 vs 7 (not valid).

drill.title: Maximum Number of Balloons
drill.statement: Using each letter of a text at most once, how many copies of the word "balloon" can be formed?
drill.approach: Count letters of the text; answer = min(b, a, l/2, o/2, n).
drill.trigger: "how many times can a word be built from these letters" → counts divided by the word's own counts.
drill.details:
**Task.** You may use each character of `text` at most once. How many complete copies of the word `"balloon"` can you form?

**Input:** a string `text`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; lowercase letters only.

**Example:** `"nlaebolko"` → `1`. `"loonbalxballpoon"` → `2`. `"leetcode"` → `0`.

cs_core.subject: OOP
cs_core.title: Polymorphism — compile time and run time

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Polymorphism** = one interface, many behaviours: the same call does different things depending on the type.
✍️ **Compile-time (static)**: method overloading (same name, different parameters). Resolved by the compiler. Java has no operator overloading or templates (it uses generics, erased at compile time).
✍️ **Run-time (dynamic)**: a superclass/interface reference calls an **overridable** method, and the actual object's override runs. The JVM resolves it at run time by looking it up via the class pointer in the object header (a per-class method-table dispatch).
✍️ In Java methods are virtual **by default**; mark a method `final` (or `static`/`private`) to make it non-overridable and statically bound.

sections.title: Java example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: Overloading vs overriding?** Overloading: same name, different parameter lists, resolved at compile time. Overriding: a subclass redefines a superclass method with the same signature, resolved at run time; annotate with `@Override`.
✍️ **Q: Does Java have destructors to worry about here?** No. Because there is no manual delete and references always point to the whole object, there is no slicing and no virtual-destructor problem; the GC handles memory.
✍️ **Q: How does the JVM dispatch an overridable call?** Through the object's class pointer (in the header) to a per-class method table — the JIT often devirtualises or uses inline caches when only one implementation is seen.
- **Q: Is there object slicing in Java?** No — a variable holds a reference to the full object, so an upcast reference still dispatches to the subclass override.
- **Q: Can you overload by return type only?** No.
